landmarks: Cité de Carcassonne
Europe's largest fortified medieval city bristles with 52 towers and double ramparts, a UNESCO fairy-tale restored by Viollet-le-Duc that seems conjured from legend.
Château Comtal
The 12th-century castle within the Cité's walls, whose ramparts walk lets visitors patrol battlements high above the Aude plain and vineyard-clad hills.
Basilique Saint-Nazaire
The Cité's 'jewel', a Romanesque-Gothic basilica whose luminous 13th-century rose windows and stained glass rank among the finest in southern France.
Pont Vieux
This graceful 14th-century stone bridge across the Aude links the lower town to the Cité, offering the classic full-frame view of the floodlit ramparts.
Canal du Midi
The plane-tree-shaded UNESCO canal of 1681 glides right past Carcassonne's rail station, perfect for barge cruises, towpath cycling, and languid Languedoc scenery.
Bastide Saint-Louis
Carcassonne's 13th-century 'new town' across the river charms with its grid of merchant mansions, lively Place Carnot, and Saturday market under Neptune's fountain.
Porte Narbonnaise
The Cité's grand twin-towered eastern gateway, flanked by a drawbridge and the statue of Dame Carcas, the legendary lady who named the city.
Cathédrale Saint-Michel
The lower town's fortified 13th-century Gothic cathedral, elevated to cathedral status in 1803, features a massive rose window and austere Languedoc lines.
Musée des Beaux-Arts de Carcassonne
A free fine-arts museum in the Bastide displaying Flemish, French, and Languedoc masters from the 17th century onward in elegant salons.
Lac de la Cavayère
A pine-ringed recreational lake minutes from the Cité, where sandy beaches, swimming platforms, and treetop adventure courses cool off summer sightseeing days.

train.note: Carcassonne station sits on the Bordeaux-Sete main line at the north edge of the lower town, about 20 minutes' walk from the medieval Cite. Direct TGV and Intercites services reach Toulouse in about an hour, Narbonne in 30 minutes and Paris in around 5-6 hours, with regional liO trains filling in the rest. There is no direct train to Spain: the former Barcelona-Toulouse TGV via Narbonne and Carcassonne no longer runs, so you must change, usually at Narbonne or Perpignan, and often again at the border. Regional liO fares are capped at a low flat rate within Occitanie, which makes short hops very cheap.

bus.note: No international coach calls at Carcassonne itself; for cross-border buses use Toulouse or Narbonne, both about an hour away, where FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) and BlaBlaCar Bus (https://www.blablacar.com/bus) run to Barcelona and Andorra. Locally, Cars liO regional coaches (https://www.lio-occitanie.fr/) serve Narbonne, Castelnaudary, Limoux, Quillan and the Aude villages from the stops beside the railway station, with tickets bought on board. A shuttle bus links the airport, 3 km away, to the station and the Cite for a few euros. Journey times are slow compared with the train, so the coach is mainly useful for villages the railway misses.

ferry.note: Carcassonne is inland on the Canal du Midi and has no ferry service. Barge and hotel-boat cruises and self-drive canal boat hire operate from the jetty by the Pont Marengo near the station, but these are leisure trips rather than transport, and most run only from spring to autumn. The nearest sea ports are Port-Vendres and Sete, both around two hours away.

half.name: Narbonne
half.blurb: Ancient Roman colony with a partly excavated forum, canal-side market halls and a striking unfinished Gothic cathedral.

half.name: Minerve
half.blurb: Cliff-perched Cathar stronghold village at the meeting of two river gorges in the Languedoc hills.

full.name: Peyrepertuse
full.blurb: Ruined Cathar castle stretched along a narrow rocky ridge, one of the region's most dramatic mountaintop fortresses.

notes.walk: La Cité's cobbled streets are compact and walkable (though steep in places); the Ville Basse across the Aude River is a separate 15-20 min walk or short bus/taxi ride
notes.card: Widely accepted; cash useful for small shops within La Cité
notes.safety: Very safe city, popular with visitors of all ages. Petty theft in crowded La Cité during peak season is the main concern.
notes.religion: Roman Catholic (majority); no religious affiliation (growing minority)
notes.net: Strong 4G/5G coverage citywide. Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes. ~€10-20 for a 10-20GB prepaid tourist SIM. Free wifi widely available. An Orange, SFR, or Bouygues tourist SIM or eSIM.
notes.transport: Carcassonne Airport (CCF) has budget flights from the UK and elsewhere in Europe; Toulouse-Blagnac (TLS) is a larger alternative about 1 hr away. TGV and regional trains connect to Toulouse and onward to the rest of France. Regional buses connect to nearby Languedoc towns. Well connected via the A61 motorway; parking is available near La Cité and in the Ville Basse.
